article.title: SignDrop: Unpatched Windows Zero-Day Turns Microsoft's CLFS Authentication Fix Into a SYSTEM Privilege Exploit
article.summary: Researcher Abdelhamid Naceri published a proof-of-concept exploit called SignDrop that abuses Microsoft's own CLFS authentication fix to gain SYSTEM privileges on Windows.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A newly published Windows exploit called SignDrop abuses a security mitigation Microsoft itself introduced to protect the Common Log File System (CLFS), using it instead to escalate a standard user account to full SYSTEM privileges, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-windows-signdrop-zero-day-gives-hackers-system-privileges/). Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri, who publishes under the names Nightmare Eclipse and MSNightmare, posted the proof-of-concept code to GitHub on November 10, 2026, according to [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) and [WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit-turns-microsofts-own-security-fix-against-itself-grants-system-privileges/). As of November 16, SignDrop has no dedicated CVE identifier and no official patch, according to [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/).

## What We Know

CLFS is a Windows kernel component — implemented in the clfs.sys driver — that manages logs used by applications and system services, and "parses complex log files in kernel mode," according to [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/). To close off prior CLFS-related bugs, Microsoft added cryptographic authentication codes that check whether a log file has been tampered with before Windows processes it, a mitigation that reached systems in October 2025, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-windows-signdrop-zero-day-gives-hackers-system-privileges/) and [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/). [Cybersecurity News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/windows-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) reports the mitigation reached Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 through updates released October 28, 2025, or later.

SignDrop targets how clfs.sys handles creation of a companion authentication file, ".cnpf", when a new log file is created, according to [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/). A standard user can create a log file with a specified container path, then coerce Windows Defender into opening it through Defender's signature-update RPC interface; because Defender is a privileged process, the resulting ".cnpf" signature file is created with SYSTEM-level permissions at a location the attacker controls, according to [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/) and [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/). Naceri described the result bluntly: "this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation of privileges," he told [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-windows-signdrop-zero-day-gives-hackers-system-privileges/). He separately claimed the technique "can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense mechanism, as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process," according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-windows-signdrop-zero-day-gives-hackers-system-privileges/); [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) notes that the broader claim that it works against every security product has not been independently verified.

Naceri tested SignDrop on Windows 11 26H2, an experimental Windows 11 26H2 build, and an experimental Windows Server 2025 build, and estimated that around 80% of Windows installations could be vulnerable, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-windows-signdrop-zero-day-gives-hackers-system-privileges/), [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/) and [WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit-turns-microsofts-own-security-fix-against-itself-grants-system-privileges/); outlets reporting the 80% figure stress it is Naceri's own estimate and has not been independently confirmed, per [Cybersecurity News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/windows-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/). The exposure window stems from how the CLFS mitigation rolls out: new systems enter a roughly 90-day "learning phase" during which CLFS adds authentication codes to existing log files, after which the driver switches to full enforcement, according to [Cybersecurity News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/windows-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) — meaning, in Naceri's words relayed by [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/), "you're generally vulnerable if your Windows installation is older than 90 days." [Cybersecurity News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/windows-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) notes SignDrop is a local privilege-escalation flaw that requires an attacker to already have code execution as a standard user; it cannot be triggered remotely over the internet.

Independent researchers have reproduced the exploit. Cybersecurity services provider Cyderes compiled and successfully tested the proof-of-concept, according to [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/). Separately, [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) reports that security firm 78researchlab confirmed the exploit works but found it "isn't reliable enough for operational use," adding that the published exploit chain requires Microsoft Defender to be enabled and triggers UAC prompts that make the activity noticeable.

Microsoft has acknowledged the report. In a statement carried by [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/nightmare-eclipse-drops-windows-zero-day-exploit-signdrop/), the company said: "Microsoft is actively investigating the reported vulnerability and will take the necessary steps to update impacted products as soon as possible. Microsoft Defender detects and blocks exploitation of this vulnerability and alerts on the associated privilege-escalation behavior. At this time, we have not observed exploitation in the wild." [WCCFTech](https://wccftech.com/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit-turns-microsofts-own-security-fix-against-itself-grants-system-privileges/) likewise reports Microsoft "has acknowledged the reports and is investigating the vulnerability." No source reports evidence that SignDrop has been exploited outside of the researchers' and independent testers' own reproductions.

## What We Don't Know

Microsoft has not said when a fix will ship or assigned a CVE identifier to the flaw, and the real-world reliability of the exploit outside controlled test environments remains unclear: 78researchlab's reproduction worked but was deemed unreliable for operational use, according to [Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/). The 80% vulnerable-installations estimate is Naceri's own calculation and has not been independently verified by any source cited here. It is also not established whether the antimalware-bypass technique works against security products beyond Windows Defender.

[Digital Trends](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/windows-11-signdrop-zero-day-exploit/) reports that disabling CLFS authentication is not a safe workaround, since doing so would remove the protection against the older CLFS vulnerabilities the mitigation was built to stop. Pending a Microsoft patch, keeping Windows and Defender updated remains the guidance relayed by that outlet.
